utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask the Registrar to call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is IT-95-16-PT, the Prosecutor against Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Vladimir Santic, Stipo Alilovic, Drago Josipovic, Marinko Katava and Dragan Papic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the appearances please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours, my name is Mark Harmon, I represent the Prosecutor's Office in this proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr President, I am Anto Nobilo, representing here Mr Marinko Katava.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have been seized of a motion filed by the Prosecutor for leave to withdraw the indictment against the accused Marinko Katava. We have carefully considered this motion and on behalf of my colleagues, I would like to ask the Prosecutor to explain the reasons behind this motion, the reasons why he is asking that leave to withdraw the indictment be granted by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. First off, this case was indicted under Rule 47, when the Prosecutor presented evidence to the confirming Judge that the Prosecutor was satisfied in the course of the investigations that had proceeded to date that there was sufficient evidence to provide reasonable grounds for believing that Mr Katava had committed crimes within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. Since then, there have been a number of developments. The first development, your Honours, is that during the course of the Blaskic case, a witness who testified for the Prosecution, by the name of Dr Muhamed Mujezinovic, testified that instead of being at the locations described in the indictment, Mr Katava was at a different location. In addition to that -- Mr President, your Honours, the Prosecutor has enormous confidence in the testimony of Dr Mujezinovic, a Prosecution witness in another case. In addition to that, Defence counsel has supplied the Office of the Prosecutor with a number of alibi witnesses. I have been informed by the investigators in this case that the Prosecution team analysing this case is satisfied with those alibi witnesses, and based on the alibi witnesses, in addition to the testimony of Dr Mujezinovic, the Prosecutor does not believe this case can be proved beyond reasonable doubt. When she came to that conclusion, your Honours, the Prosecutor filed a motion to withdraw the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the Defence counsel whether he would like to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr President, we have received a statement of the OTP about the withdrawal of the indictment, and the OTP has been notified of that in writing. We would not like to comment on the proceedings in this case, but that we acknowledge the facts and we acknowledge the notification that we have received from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right, so we may move to a second question we wanted to raise with the Prosecutor. If one reads the indictment, one can see that the charges against Mr Katava were very serious. In addition, you may remember that on 27th November 1997, Mr Katava joined the motion for provisional release which had been filed by other defendants and on 1st December, the Office of the Prosecutor filed the response, objecting to this motion for provisional release. This objection, of course, also related to Marinko Katava. So we are a bit puzzled by the change of attitude -- change in the position of the Prosecutor, and we are wondering why it took you so much time to come to the conclusion that the indictment ought to be withdrawn. Are there any particular reasons for this delay? He has been in detention for two months, and you had ample opportunity to revise the indictment, to scrutinise the evidence which was available to you and to come to a conclusion. On 1st December, your conclusion was that actually the indictment was not to be withdrawn and you objected, as I say, to the release of Marinko Katava.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would be glad to comment on that, your Honour. First off, Marinko Katava was a fugitive from justice for a considerable period of time before he went into custody for a period of two months. We should not lose sight of that fact. I believe that once he came into custody, the Prosecutor's Office, and shortly before he came into custody, the Prosecutor's Office again took a hard look at the evidence in this case, it reviewed it with diligence and good faith, it examined the alibi witnesses and although I was not privy to the filing of the motion in opposition to his provisional release, the fact of the matter is, Mr President, it takes time to analyse a number of alibi witnesses, it takes time to review the evidence in light of the newly emerging investigation that relates to a Defence that has been presented to the Prosecutor's Office. I can say, Judge Cassese, I would be quite confident that at the time the Prosecutor's Office opposed a provisional release, it had not made a decision -- clearly not come to the conclusion that the alibi was a viable Defence. It was after that fact, after the objection to the provisional release, and it was in the ensuing period of time when discussions continued, the investigators continued to discuss the merits of the potential alibi, and it was when the potential alibi was concluded -- it was concluded that that potential alibi was viable that the Prosecutor immediately filed her motion to withdraw the indictment. If the court is concerned that the Prosecutor was aware that this alibi was in fact a viable Defence and was in fact one that we would be coming before this court later to withdraw the indictment, the court should not concern itself with that. I am quite confident, your Honours, that the Prosecutor was not aware at that time on that date, when she filed an opposition to the provisional release, that the conclusion had been reached that Mr Katava had a viable alibi. That development took place after the opposition to the provisional release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether my colleagues would like to say anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just this, Mr Harmon. When did the doctor give evidence in Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do not have the date at all, your Honour. Whether it was before December 1st -- I am confident it was before December 1st, but there was additional investigation that needed to be done, based on the presentation of additional alibi witnesses. There had to be consultations and discussions with the investigative staff and the legal team that is associated with this particular case. Dr Mujezinovic gave testimony before December 1st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The date which is passed to me, Mr Harmon, suggests that it was in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It could well be, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. We would like now to see whether we can make a ruling from the bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make one additional factual comment to the court, because I think the court may have not a full and complete picture. After Dr Mujezinovic gave his testimony, it has been our experience that people in the Central Bosnia region, many of them have the same names; Marinko Katava, there may be more than one Marinko Katava. It has been the experience in the Blaskic case, for example, that Cazim Ahmic, Mr Nobilo remembers that witness who testified before this Chamber. There are in fact two Cazim Ahmics who have relevant evidence to that particular case, so after Dr Mujezinovic gave his testimony, the Prosecutor's Office had to go back down to Central Bosnia, had to contact Dr Mujezinovic, had to show Dr Mujezinovic a photo of this Marinko Katava so Dr Mujezinovic could confirm that this gentleman was the Marinko Katava that he testified about. So that was an additional step that the Prosecutor's Office took to ensure that the alibi that had been furnished in the testimony of Dr Mujezinovic related to the correct individual who was in custody in The Hague. I thought I should bring that to your Honours' attention as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether the Defence counsel would like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, Mr President, not at this point. I think that my client would like to have this done as soon as possible and leave here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (Pause). So we are now in a position to give our ruling. We note that Marinko Katava was indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia on 10th November 1995, the indictment being confirmed by Judge McDonald on the same date. We note that Marinko Katava has been in custody since his voluntary surrender on 6th October 1997, and that he sought provisional release on 27th November 1997, by joining the motion for provisional release filed by several of his co-accused in this matter on 14th November 1997. We consider that on 1st December 1997 -- we take note that on 1st December 1997, the Office of the Prosecutor filed its response objecting to the request of Marinko Katava and the other applicants for provisional release on a number of grounds. We note that this Trial Chamber was persuaded by the arguments raised by the Prosecution and issued a decision denying the request for provisional release on 15th December 1997. We also note the motion of the Prosecutor on 18th December, requesting leave to withdraw the indictment issued against Marinko Katava on the grounds that there is insufficient basis to justify proceeding with his prosecution on any of the counts with which he is charged within the indictment. We also note the letter submitted by the Defence counsel for Marinko Katava on 19th December 1997, stating that he supports the motion, and this support for the motion has been repeated today, now, in court by Marinko Katava's Defence counsel, Mr Nobilo. We have considered the submissions made at this public hearing which has been held in view of the urgency and extreme seriousness of the situation. We therefore, and here comes our ruling, we expect that in the future, the Prosecution will act expeditiously on matters of such fundamental importance as the liberty of the accused. We consider it to be in the interests of justice to restore Marinko Katava's right to liberty without delay. For these reasons, acting under Rule 51 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, we grant leave for the indictment against Marinko Katava to be withdrawn; we order the immediate release of Marinko Katava from the United Nations detention unit, subject to the practical arrangements to be made with the Dutch authorities. You know there are quite a few practical arrangements. Therefore we do not know whether his release may be effected right away or whether we have to wait until tomorrow morning. This is only because of practical arrangements with the Dutch authorities which we have tried to contact, and which have promised to come back to us in the next few hours. This is our ruling. I think there are no other matters, so the hearing is adjourned.
